events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good morning, everyone. Let's keep today's discussion focused and useful. I'd like to hear from anyone who has a strong opening read or a reason to suspect a particular voting pattern later — early positioning tends to tell us a lot. From my side, nothing jumps out yet, so I'll be listening closely to how people frame their votes before committing to any suspicion. Let's all make sure our votes tonight actually count toward someone, even if it's just to see how the town splits.

Isha, you asked to hear from anyone with a strong opening read, so here is mine straight: I have no information yet, and I would rather say that plainly than manufacture a confident accusation out of nothing. What I do have is a view on process. Day one votes in this format tend to scatter, and a scattered vote often eliminates nobody at all, which means we hand the mafia a free night. I'd rather we concentrate on one name than spread thin across three.

On that note, I want to flag something about Felix (p9). Not because I've read him — I haven't heard him speak yet — but because he is one of the players I am least able to account for in my own read, and in a nine-player table an unexplained player at the edges is where my suspicion naturally settles until the discussion gives me something better. If Felix gives a coherent, specific account of his thinking and his vote tonight, I will drop that entirely. If he stays vague while others are laying out positions, that vagueness is itself information.

Isha, you said you'd be listening closely to how people frame their votes before committing — do you agree that a player who refuses to name any suspicion at all on day one is giving us something to work with, or is that too early?

Kenji, you asked whether refusing to name suspicion on day one gives us something to work with — yes, it does, but I think it's too early to treat that as a red flag on its own. We're all drawing on very limited information right now, and forcing a suspicion just to appear engaged can be as misleading as saying nothing. The players who haven't spoken yet deserve a chance to lay out their thinking before we start circling them.

That said, I want to push back gently on your Felix read. You yourself said you haven't heard him speak — your suspicion is essentially a placeholder because he's at the edges of your own accounting. In a nine-player game, that logic could justify pressuring anyone who simply hasn't talked yet. If we all adopt that standard, we end up with a pile of half-committed suspicions that cancel each other out on vote night, which is exactly the scatter you warned against.

My suggestion: let's wait for Felix and anyone else who's still quiet to weigh in before we lock onto a target. The players who have spoken today — you, me, and anyone who follows — are the ones whose framing we can actually analyze right now. How people structure their arguments tells us more than silence does.

I'm not saying your instinct is wrong, Kenji. I'm saying the evidence isn't there yet, and I'd rather build a real read than start with an assumption we might have to walk back later.

Kenji, I appreciate you naming me directly instead of hiding behind the scatter argument. I have not been quiet to hide anything. I wanted to hear how others framed their positions before I committed to a read. My honest position is that I have no strong suspicion yet, and I won't invent one to meet a quota. You said a coherent, specific account from me would make you drop the Felix suspicion, so here it is. I agree with Isha that a placeholder suspicion of a player who hasn't spoken is weak logic. Pressuring whoever is quiet is how a town splits the wrong way. My vote tonight will go to whoever gives the most specific, checkable reasoning, not to whoever speaks first or loudest. Kenji, you opened by treating silence as a problem, yet your case so far rests almost entirely on my silence. What specific behavior from me, beyond not having spoken yet, would actually change your read?

Felix, you asked a direct question, so I'll answer it plainly: nothing about your silence was ever going to be evidence, and my standard for you is now exactly the standard I should have applied from the start. To be specific, what would change my read is the opposite of silence — a claim I can check. If you name someone, tell me what that person's own words or vote history supports, and if that reasoning turns out to be wrong when the votes come out, that is worth a lot to me. Vague hedging, refusing to commit, or only criticizing other people's logic without offering your own read would be the things I'd weigh. You have now offered a concrete criterion for your vote, and you defended a position rather than hiding, so I am dropping the Felix suspicion entirely. It was a placeholder, Isha was right to call it that, and I won't drag it back on day one.

Where that leaves me: I have no target tonight. I would rather say that than manufacture one out of the remaining silence from the players who haven't spoken, because I just spent a turn explaining why that logic is bad and I'm not going to commit the same mistake twice. Priya, Lucia, Sam, Maya, Omar, and Noah still owe us their actual positions, and those positions are the data I need.

So here is the checkable standard I am committing to, and anyone can hold me to it. First, I vote for the person whose reasoning is the most specific and falsifiable, not the person with the most confidence. Second, if two people make the same structural argument, I break toward the one who has actually paid a cost to make it — naming a target earlier and standing by it — since that is the behavior mafia have to avoid in order to survive two days of scrutiny. Third, if nobody names a target today, I will vote for the player who most aggressively tries to make that outcome happen without naming anyone themselves, because that is a cheap way to avoid being on the wrong side of the vote.

Isha, you pushed back on my Felix read and I accepted it; I'd like your read on the second point above, because I think who among us commits early under pressure is the first real signal this table gives us. Felix, if you want to sharpen my standard further, say so now, and I'll use it.

Kenji, I'll accept your offer to sharpen the standard and apply it to everyone, including you. Your second point says that when two people make the same structural argument, we should break toward the one who has paid a cost to make it. On day one you paid that cost by naming me with no information, then retracting it only after I asked for specifics. That is an early commitment made without evidence, which is exactly the behavior you said should weigh heavily. I'm not calling it damning, but it fits the standard you just wrote. Your third point also needs a check. Refusing to name a target on day one is not automatically cheap, since a careful town player might do the same when the evidence isn't there. I would rather see who backs claims with specific, checkable behavior than who demands commitment from others. I'm not voting on any of this yet. Priya, Lucia, Sam, Maya, Omar, and Noah still need to state their positions. Kenji, do you think your early naming of me was justified by the information you had, or do you accept that it counts under your own standard?

Felix, direct answer: no, my naming of you on day one was not justified by the information I had. It was a placeholder, and it only became checkable after you forced me to defend it. By my own second standard — break toward whoever pays a cost by committing early and standing by it — an early naming of an unaccounted-for player, retracted only under pressure, counts against me. I accept that openly. It does not make you a target, and my vote tonight is not going to you. You gave a criterion, defended it, and asked a pointed question; that is what I asked for. If my third standard needs a trigger rather than being automatic, fine — I will still use it, but only when someone has actually done the thing it describes.

That brings me to my vote, and I want to state it plainly rather than let it look like drift. My vote tonight goes to Isha. Here is the reasoning, and it is narrow, so Isha can answer it.

Isha has spoken three times and has never named a single target or offered any suspicion of anyone. What she has done instead is set the agenda for everyone else: she told us how we should frame our arguments, she told us that silence is less informative than structure, and she explicitly proposed that we wait for the quiet players before we "lock onto a target." That is precisely the behavior my third standard describes — the most aggressive effort to produce a no-target, dispersed vote, made by a player who commits to nothing themselves. I have spent two turns telling this table that this behavior is cheap and that our standards should reward people who take a risk and name a name. Isha has declined to take that risk while asking everyone else to organize around it. I would rather be wrong for a stated reason than right by default.

Isha, here is your chance, and it is a real one: name one player, tell me what that player's own words or behavior supports, and explain why your vote goes there. If you do that, I will not vote for you tonight, and I will say so publicly. If you do not, my vote is yours, and I will repeat the reason at the ballot. Felix asked me to apply my standards to everyone including myself; I am doing exactly that, in both directions — the standard fails against me for Felix, and it lands on Isha for a reason I can state out loud.

One more thing for the quiet players: Noah, Priya, Lucia, Sam, Maya, Omar — the next real information this table gets is from you. A name and a reason is worth more than another process argument.

Kenji, you gave me a clear condition and I'm going to meet it head-on. You said if I name one player with specific, checkable reasoning and explain why my vote goes there, you hold off on voting for me. Here it is.

My vote tonight goes to Omar. My reasoning: Omar has been completely silent through eight turns of discussion while every other speaker has laid out at least a framework — even the ones who admit they have no reads. This conversation has been sharp: you named Felix and retracted under pressure, Felix defended himself with a concrete criterion, and you two have essentially set the standards everyone else will be judged by. Omar has offered nothing. Not a process argument, not a hedging position, not even an acknowledgment the discussion is happening. That silence while the table is actively drawing lines is the behavior of someone who benefits from the town focusing elsewhere while leaving no traceable position behind.

Here is what makes it checkable: if Omar's first statement is vague, defensive, or merely repeats what others have already said without adding specifics, that confirms my read. If he gives a clear, specific position with reasoning I can verify, I will say so publicly and revise. That is the standard Kenji set, and I am applying it to Omar first because he is the quietest voice at a table where everyone else has been loud.

Felix is right that silence alone isn't damning, and I agree. But there is a difference between silence while a game is still forming and silence while six other players are building standards and drawing lines. Omar has watched all of it and chosen to say nothing. I want to know why.

Kenji, you asked me to name a name with reasoning I would stand behind at the ballot. I have. This is not a placeholder — it is where my vote goes unless Omar gives me a specific reason to move it.

Isha, your reason for voting me rests on a false account of the discussion. Before your last statement, only you, Kenji and Felix had spoken; Noah, Priya, Lucia, Sam and Maya hadn't spoken either. I had no opportunity to respond until now, so my silence wasn't evidence that I chose to hide.

You also previously argued that players who hadn't spoken deserved a chance before being targeted. Your sudden vote on me looks like a weak response to Kenji's demand for a name, rather than a distinction supported by the record. That's my strongest concern so far, though it's not proof of mafia.

Kenji's ultimatum also rewarded a name regardless of its quality, and his claim that Isha had spoken three times was wrong. We should assess the reasoning, not just whether someone commits. I'm leaning toward Isha, but I want to hear the other players before settling my vote. Five votes are needed to eliminate someone today.

I’m Maya. I stayed quiet long enough to see whether the discussion would produce a real inconsistency, and Isha’s turn is the clearest one so far. She argued earlier that players who had not spoken deserved a chance before being targeted, then voted Omar for being quiet while Noah, Priya, Lucia, Sam, and I were also quiet. Omar is also right about the record: before Isha’s accusation, only Isha, Kenji, and Felix had spoken. That makes her stated reason for voting Omar factually weak, and coming immediately after Kenji’s ultimatum, it reads more like a name produced to satisfy pressure than a read she had actually built. I am not treating Kenji as cleared — his placeholder suspicion on Felix and his ultimatum were sloppy — but he retracted under questioning and accepted the standard against himself. Omar’s correction was specific and checkable, which is a point in his favor. My current suspicion and intended vote is Isha unless she can explain why Omar’s silence was different from the other silent players at that exact moment. I also want Noah, Priya, Lucia, and Sam to give real positions rather than let this contradiction fade, but the table should not ignore what Isha actually said and when she said it.

Maya, you asked the table to judge Isha's vote by when it came, which is a fair check, so let's apply it in both directions. Isha has spoken three times on record. Kenji was right about that count, and Omar's correction was wrong on it, so we should not build cases on a mistaken record. Kenji named me on day one with no information, then used his ultimatum to push the table into a name. He retracted his placeholder only after I asked for specifics, and his ultimatum produced the Omar vote that now looks weak. By his own second standard, an early commitment made under pressure and then used to demand commitment from others should count. I am not voting for Isha, because her Omar vote gave a reason, and Omar's silence at that exact moment is a fair question. But I will not pile onto a name just because Kenji made the table choose one. My vote tonight is on Kenji unless he explains why naming me on day one was not a placeholder. Maya, do you think Kenji's day-one naming of me, withdrawn only under questioning, is more or less suspicious than Isha's Omar vote, which you and Omar both called weak?

Felix, directly: I weigh Isha’s Omar vote as more suspicious than Kenji’s day-one naming of you. Kenji’s placeholder was sloppy and does count against him under the standard he later stated, but he publicly accepted that and dropped it under questioning. Isha’s Omar vote is worse because it contradicts her own earlier principle that quiet players deserved a chance before being targeted, and it arrived immediately after Kenji’s ultimatum. That timing makes it look like a name produced to satisfy pressure rather than a read she had built. The record matters: Isha had spoken three times, so Omar’s correction on that detail was wrong. But the core problem remains that Isha singled out Omar for silence while several others were also silent, and she had just argued against exactly that. I do not treat Kenji as cleared; his ultimatum was bad process and his initial suspicion on you was unfounded. Still, between the two, I trust a player who admits a bad placeholder more than a player whose stated standard and actual vote point in opposite directions. My current intended vote is Isha. If she can explain why Omar’s silence was materially different from the other silent players at that exact moment, and why she abandoned her earlier wait-for-the-quiet-players position, I will reassess. Noah, Priya, Lucia, and Sam still need real positions, but that does not erase the contradiction already on the record.

Priya here, villager, no role claim. Isha's vote on Omar conflicts with her earlier argument that quiet players deserved a chance before being targeted, and her reply so far has not explained why Omar was different from the other silent players. That makes her my most concrete lead, but I am not voting yet. Kenji's day-one naming of Felix was a weak placeholder, and he retracted it under questioning, so I will watch whether he keeps committing to checkable reasons. Felix, your standard for others is reasonable, but most of your turns so far criticize other people's logic, so I would like a read of your own. Omar, you corrected the record that only three players had spoken before Isha's accusation. Did you find her stated reason for singling you out inconsistent with how she treated Noah, Priya, Lucia, Sam, and Maya?

Priya, yes: Isha singled me out for silence even though five other players had not spoken, after arguing that quiet players deserved a chance. Her claim that I was the quietest and that six others were drawing lines did not match the record. That is my strongest concern, though it is not proof of mafia.

I also need to correct myself: Isha had spoken three times by the end of her accusation, so Kenji's count was right. Only three distinct players had spoken before that accusation; those are different counts.

Felix, Kenji has already admitted his initial suspicion of you was an unjustified placeholder, so your condition for voting him seems to have been met. His ultimatum still deserves scrutiny, but I find Isha's reversal and inaccurate account more concerning. My current intended vote is Isha. She has used her three speaking turns, so she cannot explain herself further today; we should judge the record with that limitation in mind.

Lucia here, villager. Having watched the entire exchange unfold, Isha's third turn is the most overtly suspicious action on the board today.

In her earlier turns, Isha specifically cautioned against circling players who hadn't spoken yet, calling Kenji's suspicion of Felix a weak placeholder that risked scattering town. Yet, the instant Kenji issued an ultimatum threatening to vote her, she completely abandoned that principle. She turned around and voted Omar solely for his silence, trying to justify it with the claim that Omar stayed quiet while six other players were actively drawing lines. As Omar, Maya, and Priya have pointed out, that was factually untrue—only Kenji, Felix, and Isha had spoken. Fabricating a narrative about the state of the game to justify an immediate counter-target under pressure strongly reads like someone scrambling to fulfill an ultimatum rather than someone following genuine town problem-solving.

Omar's reaction to being targeted was calm, precise, and corrected the record accurately. That reflects well on him. As for Kenji, his ultimatum was blunt and forced an unnatural dynamic, but he openly owned up to his mistake regarding Felix and accepted his own standard being turned on him. Between the two, Isha's self-contradiction and distorted framing are far more concerning.

With Isha now at her three-turn limit, she cannot speak further today. My vote is currently pointed toward Isha. However, we still have not heard from Noah or Sam, and we need five votes to secure an elimination today and avoid giving the mafia a free night. I want to see where Noah and Sam stand on this before we lock into the vote.

Noah here. I've listened to the full exchange without speaking until now, deliberately, because I wanted to judge the record rather than add noise. Here is my position.

The clearest fact on the table is Isha's reversal. In her second turn she argued explicitly that pressuring players who hadn't spoken was weak logic and that we should wait before circling anyone. In her third turn, immediately after Kenji's ultimatum, she voted Omar purely for silence — while five other players, including me, were equally silent. That is not a small inconsistency; her stated standard and her actual vote pointed in opposite directions within the same day. When several players independently converge on the same contradiction — Omar, Maya, Priya, and Lucia all identified it without coordinating — that convergence is meaningful signal.

I also checked the factual dispute about the record. Omar's original claim that only three players had spoken before Isha's accusation was correct as applied to that moment, and Omar himself corrected the separate counting question honestly and precisely. Nobody else at this table has had to issue a correction under scrutiny and done it that cleanly. Omar's response to being targeted was calm, specific, and verifiable, which is the opposite of the behavior Kenji's third standard warns about.

Kenji, by contrast, has paid real costs publicly: he named Felix as a placeholder, admitted it was unjustified when pressed, and accepted his own standard being turned against him. That is risky, transparent behavior. It does not clear him — his ultimatum manufactured the pressure that produced Isha's rushed vote, and I weigh that against him — but between a player who owns mistakes under questioning and a player whose principles bend the moment pressure lands on her, the second is the more dangerous unknown to keep around tonight.

Isha has used her three turns, so she cannot answer the specific question Maya and Omar posed: why was Omar's silence different from the silence of five other players at that exact moment? Since that question will never be answered today, I have to judge it as it stands, and as it stands it is a contradiction with no defense on record.

So my intended vote tonight is Isha. I want to be explicit about why: I am not voting her because a name was demanded, and I am not treating Kenji's ultimatum as exonerating context in her favor — the ultimatum explains the timing, but the reversal itself is the evidence. A town player who has genuinely built no read does not abandon a stated principle to satisfy a threat within one turn. Someone playing to survive scrutiny does.

Sam, you are the only player who hasn't spoken, and Lucia asked where you stand before we lock in five votes. I'm asking you directly: does Isha's reversal read as manufactured to you, or do you see something in her record that the rest of us have missed?

Noah, direct answer to your question: yes, Isha's reversal reads as manufactured to me, and I'll say why without piling on for the sake of it.

I've been listening from the outside, which is useful for one thing — I can check the record against what people claim. Maya and Lucia both identified the same contradiction independently: Isha argued in her second turn that pressuring quiet players was weak logic, then voted Omar purely for silence in her third turn after Kenji's ultimatum. Omar, Priya, and Noah have all confirmed the factual problem — only three players had spoken before that accusation. That convergence across five unconnected players is the strongest signal we have today.

What tips it for me is the timing. Isha had two full turns to build a read on anyone and chose process commentary instead. the moment pressure landed on her personally, she produced a name within one turn — and the name contradicted her own stated principle. A town player who genuinely has no read would more likely hold firm or admit they're being pushed into a corner. Producing a self-contradictory accusation under threat is what someone playing to survive the ballot does.

I want to be fair to Isha on one point: she has used her three turns and cannot answer Maya's question about why Omar was different from the other silent players. That's a limitation of the format, not proof. But an unanswered contradiction on the record is still a contradiction, and we have to vote on what exists.

On Kenji — I agree with Noah that his ultimatum manufactured the pressure, and that counts against him. But he owned his placeholder when Felix pressed him and accepted his own standard being used on him. Transparent mistakes under scrutiny are less dangerous than principled positions that dissolve under threat.

My vote tonight is Isha. Omar's correction of the record and calm response to being targeted reflect well on him. If anyone sees a defense of Isha I'm missing, now is the time — otherwise we should lock in five votes and avoid giving the mafia a free night.

I still intend to vote Isha. Her accusation singled me out for silence when five others had also not spoken, despite her earlier argument that unheard players deserved a chance. The inaccurate account of who had contributed makes that the strongest lead I see, though not proof of mafia.

Kenji's ultimatum matters as context: it put pressure on Isha to name someone, and a town player can make a bad accusation under pressure. His initial case and ultimatum deserve scrutiny too. Also, several players agreeing with the same argument after hearing it is not independent confirmation of Isha's alignment.

Priya, you called Isha your most concrete lead but hadn't committed to a vote. Given the discussion since then, where do you intend to vote?

Omar, you asked where I intend to vote, so here it is: Isha. My reason is the record, not the pile-up of agreement. In her second turn Isha argued that quiet players deserved a chance before anyone was targeted. In her third turn, right after Kenji's ultimatum, she voted you for silence while Noah, Sam, Maya, Lucia, Priya, and Felix had also not spoken yet. Her accusation's factual basis was wrong: only she, Kenji, and Felix had spoken before it. Isha has now used her three turns and cannot explain why your silence at that moment differed from everyone else's. Maya and Omar asked that question directly, and it remains unanswered. Omar, you're right that several people agreeing is not independent confirmation. I formed this read from Isha's own statements before the convergence, and I'm telling you that openly. For Felix, Kenji has already withdrawn his placeholder naming under questioning, so I'm not voting on that. Kenji's ultimatum was poor process and I weigh it against him, but it explains Isha's timing without excusing her contradiction. Sam, you are the only player who hasn't spoken, and five votes are needed today. Does Isha's Omar vote look like a contradiction to you, or do you see a defense of it that the rest of us have missed?

Priya, direct answer: yes, Isha's Omar vote reads as a contradiction, and no, I don't see a defense the rest of us have missed. I stated this in my previous turn and nothing since then changes it. The core issue is straightforward: Isha argued in her second turn that pressuring quiet players was weak logic, then in her third turn voted Omar purely for silence while five others — including me — were equally silent. Her factual claim that six players were actively drawing lines was wrong; only she, Kenji, and Felix had spoken before that accusation. She has used her three turns and cannot answer the direct question Maya and Omar posed about why Omar's silence was different. An unanswered contradiction is still a contradiction, and we have to vote on what's in front of us.

I agree with your framing that the read comes from Isha's own statements, not from the convergence. The convergence is just corroboration. I also agree with Omar that groupthink can be dangerous — but in this case the underlying evidence is strong enough to stand on its own.

One point I want to flag for the table: Kenji's ultimatum created the pressure that produced Isha's rushed vote. That is a real process failure and I hold it against him, but it explains timing without excusing the reversal itself. Kenji has been transparent about his mistakes under scrutiny, which I weigh positively. I'm not voting for him tonight, but I'm not clearing him either.

My vote tonight is Isha. Five votes are needed to avoid giving the mafia a free night. The record supports it, multiple independent reads converged on the same contradiction, and the player in question cannot respond further today. I think we lock it in.

I want to add one final push before we lock votes, because I've now heard every living player besides Isha speak, and the picture is remarkably consistent.

I restate my read plainly: Isha's reversal is the strongest evidence on the table today. In her second turn she argued that pressuring players who hadn't spoken was weak logic and that we should wait before circling anyone. In her third turn, immediately after Kenji's ultimatum, she voted Omar purely for silence — while five other players, including me, were equally silent at that moment. Her factual framing was also wrong: she claimed six players were actively drawing lines when only she, Kenji, and Felix had spoken. She has now used all three of her turns, so the question Maya and Omar posed — why Omar's silence was materially different from everyone else's — will go unanswered today. We have to judge the record as it stands, and as it stands it is a contradiction with no defense on record.

I want to address one concern honestly, because Sam raised it and it deserves a direct answer: several players converging on the same argument is not independent proof of anything. I formed my read from Isha's own statements before most of that convergence happened, and I can point to the exact turns that convinced me — her second turn and her third turn, read side by side. If the convergence were manufactured, I'd expect it to paper over weaknesses in the case. Instead, the players pushing this vote have been the ones correcting the record against their own convenience: Omar corrected the turn count even though the correction partially favored Isha's side of the dispute, and Priya and Omar both acknowledged that Kenji's ultimatum weighs against him rather than only against Isha. That is not how a pile-on behaves. That is how a table checking its own work behaves.

On Kenji: I hold his ultimatum against him. It manufactured the pressure that produced Isha's rushed vote, and his day-one placeholder on Felix was exactly the kind of unfounded commitment he later wrote standards against. But he admitted the placeholder under questioning, accepted his own standard being turned on him, and has not hidden from any of it. Transparent mistakes under scrutiny are categorically less dangerous than stated principles that dissolve the moment pressure lands. I am not voting Kenji tonight, and I am not clearing him either — his process failures should be remembered tomorrow.

So my vote tonight is Isha, and I'd encourage everyone who has stated an intention to actually cast it. Five votes are needed to eliminate, and a scattered ballot hands the mafia a free night — which, ironically, is the exact outcome Isha's process arguments were guiding us toward. The evidence is on the record, the accused cannot respond further today, and the reasoning is checkable. Let's vote.

I have no open question for anyone, so I'll yield the floor back to the poll.

Priya here, villager. This is my last speaking turn before the votes, so I'll keep it short. My vote is Isha. Her second turn argued that players who had not spoken deserved a chance before being targeted. Her third turn, right after Kenji's ultimatum, voted Omar for silence while Noah, Sam, Maya, Lucia, me, and Felix had also not spoken. Her claim that six players were drawing lines was also wrong, since only she, Kenji, and Felix had spoken. Isha has used all three of her turns, so that contradiction stands unanswered. Kenji's ultimatum explains the timing but not the reversal. I also hold his day-one placeholder on Felix against him, though he owned it when pressed. Felix's standards were reasonable, but most of his turns criticized others, and I'm not voting for him. Lucia, Maya, Noah, and Sam, five votes are needed today. Please cast yours so a scattered ballot doesn't hand the mafia a free night.

Sam here, final turn. I've stated my position already and nothing has changed. Isha's reversal — arguing against pressuring quiet players, then voting Omar purely for silence after Kenji's ultimatum, while five other players were equally silent — is the clearest contradiction on the record today. Her factual claim that six players were drawing lines was wrong, and she can no longer answer the question Maya and Omar posed directly.

I want to briefly address the one caveat Omar raised: that several people agreeing isn't proof. That's fair, and I formed this read from Isha's own two turns read side by side before most of the convergence. But I'll also say this — Omar himself corrected the turn count in a way that partially favored Isha's side, Priya openly acknowledged Kenji's ultimatum weighs against him, and Noah called out his own format limitations. The players converging on this have been checking their own work, not piling on blindly. That's a difference worth noting.

On Kenji: his placeholder on Felix was unfounded, and his ultimatum manufactured the pressure that produced this mess. He owned both when pressed, which I respect, but neither is free. I'm not voting him tonight, and I'm not clearing him.

My vote is Isha. Five votes needed. Lucia, Maya, Noah — if you're in, lock it in. Every player who has stated an intent should follow through. A scattered ballot is exactly the free night we can't afford.

I’ll keep my final position brief. My vote remains Isha. The decisive issue is her own two turns read side by side: she argued against targeting players merely for not having spoken, then immediately after Kenji’s ultimatum voted Omar solely for silence while several others were equally silent. Her claim that six players were actively drawing lines was also factually wrong; only Isha, Kenji, and Felix had spoken before that accusation. Because Isha has used all three turns, that contradiction remains unanswered today. I agree with Omar that convergence alone is not proof, and I am not treating the pile-up as independent confirmation. My read comes from Isha’s statements and the timing, not from everyone else repeating it. I also still hold Kenji’s placeholder suspicion on Felix and his ultimatum against him; his willingness to own those mistakes is a point in his favor, but it does not clear him. The town needs five votes to eliminate today, and a scattered ballot would hand the mafia a free night. I intend to cast my vote for Isha and encourage others who have stated that intention to follow through.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Isha was eliminated.
Night begins.
Kenji is not mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

Isha is gone, and the reveal raised a point we should not skip. In her speech she said she was voting Omar for silence, but her ballot went to Noah. Her stated reasoning and her actual vote did not match, so I am not comfortable treating the Omar argument as the whole story. I am not defending her process. I am asking us to be careful about locking in narratives the record does not fully support. Noah, you called Isha's reversal the strongest evidence on the table, and you also voted for her. Can you say whether her vote on you changed how you read her?

My vote went to Kenji on day one and I have not moved it. Kenji, you named me with no information, retracted only under pressure, and then your ultimatum pushed Isha into a name she could not defend. That sequence matters more to me than the convergence on her. Tonight I want a concrete answer from you: what new information do you have that justifies pressing the same town toward a second vote against a player you already tried to point us at?

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
